Report: Shortlist of African kingdoms matching the clue, with evidence and assessment Task recap - Clue: “This kingdom lives in the central region of an African country and is known for its rich cultural heritage. From the 19th to the 20th century, this kingdom had major conflicts with a global superpower.” - Deliverables for each candidate: (a) country and whether located in that country’s central region; (b) brief note on renowned cultural heritage; (c) specific major conflicts with a global superpower spanning late 19th to early 20th century (identify superpower and date range); (d) recognized founder or cofounder names (especially any phrased as having ‘helped cofound’ the kingdom); and (e) citations from reliable sources. - Priority candidates: Ashanti (Ghana), Buganda (Uganda), Bunyoro (Uganda), Luba (DRC), Bamum/Bamoun (Cameroon), Merina (Madagascar), Mossi (Burkina Faso), Zulu (South Africa), Benin (Nigeria), Sokoto (Nigeria). Include other plausible matches if found. - Output: concise comparative table/summary + short narrative assessment of which candidates best fit all clues. What was done (concise process summary with sources gathered) - Verified Asante/Ashanti using Encyclopaedia Britannica (location and British conflict through 1902); UNESCO (Asante Traditional Buildings near Kumasi for heritage); and Britannica biography of Okomfo Anokye for explicit “cofounder” phrasing. • Source captures: - “Kumasi, city, south-central Ghana.” (Britannica – Kumasi) - “Near Kumasi… last remaining testimony of the great Asante civilization…” (UNESCO – Asante Traditional Buildings) - “On January 1, 1902, Asante was formally declared a British crown colony…” (Britannica – Asante empire) - “Okomfo Anokye… cofounder of the Asante empire.” (Britannica – Okomfo Anokye) - Verified Buganda’s central-region heritage via UNESCO (Kasubi Tombs in Kampala District; “major spiritual centre”), and used Britannica’s Uganda overview for late-19th British protectorate context (conflict timeline across century boundary is standard; exact subpage details not scraped in-session). - Verified Merina’s central highlands location and heritage via UNESCO (Royal Hill of Ambohimanga in the ‘Hautes Terres Centrales’; religious capital of the kingdom in the 19th century; French colonial actions in 1897). Britannica country-history pages for the 1895–1896 conquest and Menalamba rebellion (1895–1897) could not be scraped in-session due to site restrictions; these timelines are widely documented. - Considered additional candidates (Mossi, Luba, Sokoto, Bunyoro, Bamum, Zulu, Benin). These were assessed at a high level for match to the three clues; direct citations for them were not retrieved in-session (flagged where evidence is incomplete). Comparative shortlist (evidence-backed candidates) 1) Ashanti (Asante), Ghana - (a) Country and central-region location: - Ghana. The Asante capital Kumasi is in “south-central Ghana.” Quote: “Kumasi, city, south-central Ghana.” (Britannica – Kumasi: https://www.britannica.com/place/Kumasi) - (b) Renowned cultural heritage: - UNESCO-inscribed Asante Traditional Buildings, “Near Kumasi… last remaining testimony of the great Asante civilization… The buildings… are the last surviving examples of a significant traditional style of architecture that epitomized the … Asante Kingdom.” (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/35) - (c) Major conflicts with a global superpower (spanning late 19th–early 20th century): - Global superpower: Great Britain. Anglo-Asante wars culminated with annexation crossing the century boundary. Quote: “on January 1, 1902, Asante was formally declared a British crown colony…” (Britannica – Asante empire: https://www.britannica.com/place/Asante-empire) - (d) Recognized founder/cofounder: - Osei Tutu (founding Asantehene); Okomfo Anokye explicitly as “cofounder of the Asante empire.” (Britannica – Okomfo Anokye: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Okomfo-Anokye) - (e) Citations: - Britannica – Asante empire: https://www.britannica.com/place/Asante-empire - Britannica – Kumasi: https://www.britannica.com/place/Kumasi - UNESCO – Asante Traditional Buildings: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/35 - Britannica – Okomfo Anokye: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Okomfo-Anokye 2) Buganda, Uganda - (a) Country and central-region location: - Uganda. Core royal site is within Kampala District (Uganda’s Central Region). UNESCO: “The Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi constitute a site embracing almost 30 ha of hillside within Kampala district.” (UNESCO – Kasubi Tombs: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1022) - (b) Renowned cultural heritage: - Kasubi Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage): “major spiritual centre for the Baganda… a masterpiece… exceptional surviving example of an architectural style developed by the powerful Buganda Kingdom since the 13th Century.” (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1022) - (c) Major conflicts with a global superpower (spanning late 19th–early 20th century): - Global superpower: Great Britain. Uganda protectorate established in the late 19th century with settlement and agreements crossing into the early 20th century. - Britannica (Uganda overview, Top Questions): “Great Britain declared the Uganda protectorate in the late 1800s.” (https://www.britannica.com/place/Uganda) - Note: Specifics such as Mwanga II’s 1897–1899 resistance and the 1900 Uganda Agreement are standard in authoritative histories; direct subpage quotes were not captured this session (should be cited from Britannica History subpages or equivalent). - (d) Recognized founder/cofounder: - Tradition identifies Kato Kintu as the first Kabaka (founder). A direct encyclopedia citation (e.g., Britannica – Buganda) should be added for formal documentation (not scraped this session). - (e) Citations: - UNESCO – Kasubi Tombs: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1022 - Britannica – Uganda (overview with protectorate context): https://www.britannica.com/place/Uganda - Founder citation to add (not scraped): Britannica – Buganda. 3) Merina (Imerina), Madagascar - (a) Country and central-region location: - Madagascar. UNESCO places the royal hill in the central highlands and Antananarivo region. Quotes: - “civilization which developed in the ‘Hautes Terres Centrales’ in Madagascar between the 15th and 19th centuries…” and - “Religious capital and sacred town of the kingdom of Madagascar in the 19th century… among the fortified groups of the Imerina (region of Antananarivo).” (UNESCO – Royal Hill of Ambohimanga: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/950) - (b) Renowned cultural heritage: - Royal Hill of Ambohimanga (UNESCO World Heritage): royal city, tombs, sacred places; exceptional architectural ensemble (Rova); core of Malagasy royal identity. (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/950) - (c) Major conflicts with a global superpower (spanning late 19th–early 20th century): - Global superpower: France. French conquest and annexation occurred in the 1890s with resistance spanning across the century boundary; UNESCO also notes colonial actions in 1897: “the sacred wooden houses… demolished by the French colonial authorities… the mortal remains… removed from the site in 1897…” (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/950) - Note: Full conflict chronology (e.g., 1895–1896 conquest; Menalamba rebellion 1895–1897; early 1900s pacification) should be cited from an encyclopedia or academic history; Britannica access was restricted during this session. - (d) Recognized founder/cofounder: - Andriamanelo (traditionally credited with founding Imerina) and Andrianampoinimerina (18th–19th century unifier). Direct Britannica citations can be added (not scraped this session). - (e) Citations: - UNESCO – Royal Hill of Ambohimanga: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/950 - Additional standard references to add (not scraped): Britannica – Madagascar (History), Britannica – Andriamanelo, Britannica – Andrianampoinimerina. Additional candidates (plausible but with gaps relative to the three clues and/or not fully cited in-session) - Mossi kingdoms (Burkina Faso): Historically centered on the central plateau (around present-day Ouagadougou), rich heritage; French conquest circa 1896 with consolidation into early 1900s. Needs direct citations (e.g., Britannica – Mossi; Burkina Faso history). Fit: likely yes (central location, heritage, conflict across the boundary). Citation gaps remain. - Luba kingdom (DRC): Heartland in south-central/central DRC (Katanga–Kasai), rich Luba cultural heritage; faced Congo Free State/Belgian colonial violence from late 19th into 20th century. Needs direct citations (e.g., Britannica – Luba; DRC history). Fit: likely yes; location wording should be verified. - Sokoto Caliphate (Nigeria): Centered in the northwest but extended into parts of central Nigeria; British conquest culminated in 1903 (cross-century). Culturally significant. Fit: good on conflicts and heritage; “central-region” criterion may be debatable; needs exact location phrasing and citations (Britannica – Sokoto; Nigeria history). - Bunyoro (Uganda): Rich heritage; intense wars with Britain (1890s–early 1900s), but geographic core is mid-west Uganda (not central). Likely fails central-region criterion. - Bamum/Bamoun (Cameroon): Renowned heritage (Foumban palace, Sultan Njoya’s script) in Cameroon’s West Region (not the Central Region). Colonial transitions under Germany/France; not typically framed as prolonged “major conflicts” across the boundary. Likely fails central-region criterion. - Zulu (South Africa): Rich heritage; conflicts with Britain (1879) and rebellion (1906) but homeland is in eastern South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal), not central. Fails central-region criterion. - Benin Kingdom (Nigeria): Rich heritage (Benin Bronzes); British punitive expedition in 1897, but located in southern Nigeria (Edo State), not central; conflicts do not extend meaningfully across the century boundary (annexation in 1897). Fails central-region criterion. Concise comparative summary (fit to the three clues) - Strongest matches (all three clues met with in-session citations): - Ashanti (Ghana): Central-region location anchored by Kumasi (south-central Ghana); UNESCO-recognized heritage near Kumasi; Anglo-Asante conflict culminating in 1902 (Britain). Cofounder wording present (Okomfo Anokye). - Buganda (Uganda): Heritage core in Kampala (Central Region) with UNESCO Kasubi Tombs; British protectorate established in late 19th century with settlement into early 20th. Founder name (Kato Kintu) is standard but needs direct citation addition. - Merina (Madagascar): Central highlands (Imerina/Antananarivo region) and UNESCO-recognized royal heritage; French colonial actions noted in 1897 with broader conquest/resistance spanning the boundary (add full conflict dates via a standard source). - Plausible matches (require additional direct citations for precise location wording and/or founder phrasing): Mossi (Burkina Faso), Luba (DRC), Sokoto (Nigeria). - Weak or non-matches on central-region criterion: Bunyoro (mid-west Uganda), Bamum (West Region, Cameroon), Zulu (eastern South Africa), Benin (southern Nigeria). Short narrative assessment of best fits - Ashanti (Asante) is the clearest match. Its political and cultural core at Kumasi is in south-central Ghana, directly satisfying the “central region” cue; its cultural heritage is internationally recognized (UNESCO Asante Traditional Buildings near Kumasi); and its sustained engagements with a global superpower (Great Britain) extended across the century boundary, culminating in British crown colony status on January 1, 1902. Uniquely, it also has authoritative “cofounder” phrasing for Okomfo Anokye alongside Osei Tutu, addressing the “helped cofound” request. - Buganda also aligns closely with the clue. The Kasubi Tombs in Kampala (Uganda’s Central Region) embody the kingdom’s rich, living heritage. British expansion and the formation of the protectorate in the late 19th century, with settlement into the early 20th century, meet the cross-century conflict criterion. Founder name (Kato Kintu) is well known; add a direct encyclopedia citation to finalize. - Merina (Imerina) fits strongly for central-region location (central highlands, Antananarivo region), deep royal heritage (Royal Hill of Ambohimanga), and conflict with France around the turn of the century (annexation in the 1890s, resistance, and documented colonial actions in 1897). Add a standard encyclopedia citation for the 1895–1897 conflict timeline to complete the entry. Key source excerpts (verbatim) and URLs - “Kumasi, city, south-central Ghana.” (Britannica – Kumasi: https://www.britannica.com/place/Kumasi) - “Near Kumasi, a group of traditional buildings are the last remaining testimony of the great Asante civilization…” (UNESCO – Asante Traditional Buildings: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/35) - “On January 1, 1902, Asante was formally declared a British crown colony…” (Britannica – Asante empire: https://www.britannica.com/place/Asante-empire) - “Okomfo Anokye… was a fetish priest … and cofounder of the Asante empire…” (Britannica – Okomfo Anokye: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Okomfo-Anokye) - “The Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi constitute a site embracing almost 30 ha of hillside within Kampala district… The site is the major spiritual centre for the Baganda…” (UNESCO – Kasubi Tombs: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1022) - “Great Britain declared the Uganda protectorate in the late 1800s.” (Britannica – Uganda, Top Questions: https://www.britannica.com/place/Uganda) - “The Royal Hill of Ambohimanga constitutes an exceptional witness to the civilization which developed in the ‘Hautes Terres Centrales’ in Madagascar… Religious capital and sacred town of the kingdom of Madagascar in the 19th century… among the fortified groups of the Imerina (region of Antananarivo)… the sacred wooden houses… were demolished by the French colonial authorities… the mortal remains… removed from the site in 1897…” (UNESCO – Royal Hill of Ambohimanga: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/950) Caveats and next steps (if further precision is required) - Buganda conflicts: Add specific dates and events (e.g., Mwanga II’s 1897–1899 resistance; 1900 Uganda Agreement) with direct citations from Britannica (Uganda history subpages) or academic histories. - Merina conflicts: Add Britannica (Madagascar – History) or equivalent academic citations detailing the 1895–1896 conquest, Menalamba rebellion (1895–1897), and early 1900s pacification. - Founders for Buganda (Kato Kintu), Mossi (Yennenga/Ouedraogo traditions), Luba (Kongolo Mwamba/Ilunga Mbidi), Sokoto (Usman dan Fodio): provide direct encyclopedia citations if included as finalists. - For Mossi, Luba, Sokoto: verify exact “central-region” phrasing and provide precise conflict date ranges with reliable citations. FINAL ANSWER (concise comparative table and summary) A) Comparative table (top evidence-backed candidates) - Ashanti (Asante), Ghana - Central-region? Yes. Capital Kumasi is in “south-central Ghana.” (Britannica: https://www.britannica.com/place/Kumasi) - Cultural heritage: UNESCO Asante Traditional Buildings near Kumasi; “last remaining testimony of the great Asante civilization” and “epitomized the… Asante Kingdom.” (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/35) - Conflicts (superpower; dates): Great Britain; Anglo-Asante conflicts through “January 1, 1902” crown colony declaration (spans the century boundary). (Britannica: https://www.britannica.com/place/Asante-empire) - Founder/cofounder: Osei Tutu (founder); Okomfo Anokye “cofounder of the Asante empire.” (Britannica: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Okomfo-Anokye) - Citations: As above. - Buganda, Uganda - Central-region? Yes. Kasubi Tombs “within Kampala district” (Central Region); “major spiritual centre.” (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1022) - Cultural heritage: Kasubi Tombs, UNESCO-inscribed; masterpiece of Ganda palace architecture; living ritual traditions. (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1022) - Conflicts (superpower; dates): Great Britain; “Great Britain declared the Uganda protectorate in the late 1800s” with settlement/agreements into early 20th century (e.g., 1900 Agreement). (Britannica overview: https://www.britannica.com/place/Uganda) [Add subpage citation for exact dates as needed] - Founder/cofounder: Kato Kintu (traditional founder; add Britannica – Buganda citation). - Citations: As above. - Merina (Imerina), Madagascar - Central-region? Yes. Royal hill in the “Hautes Terres Centrales” (central highlands); among Imerina (Antananarivo region). (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/950) - Cultural heritage: Royal Hill of Ambohimanga (UNESCO) – royal city, tombs, sacred places; religious capital of the kingdom in the 19th century. (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/950) - Conflicts (superpower; dates): France; annexation in 1890s with resistance around century boundary; UNESCO notes colonial actions in 1897 (removal of remains; demolition). (UNESCO: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/950) [Add Britannica – Madagascar History for 1895–1897 conflicts and early 1900s pacification] - Founder/cofounder: Andriamanelo (founder), Andrianampoinimerina (unifier) [add direct encyclopedia citations]. - Citations: As above. B) Additional plausible matches (need targeted citations to finalize) - Mossi (Burkina Faso): Central plateau location; French conquest 1896 with consolidation into 1900s; rich court/arts heritage. [Citations to add: Britannica – Mossi; Burkina Faso history] - Luba (DRC): South-central/central location; Congo Free State/Belgian colonial violence late 19th–early 20th; renowned Luba arts and institutions. [Citations to add: Britannica – Luba; DRC history] - Sokoto (Nigeria): Northwestern center with reach into central areas; British conquest by 1903; major Islamic scholarly/cultural heritage. [Citations to add: Britannica – Sokoto; Nigeria history] - Less likely on central-region criterion: Bunyoro (mid-west Uganda), Bamum (West Region, Cameroon), Zulu (eastern South Africa), Benin (southern Nigeria). Best-fit narrative - Ashanti (Asante) is the strongest single match: central-region core (Kumasi, south-central Ghana), world-recognized cultural heritage near the capital, and sustained Anglo-Asante conflicts culminating in 1902. The explicit “cofounder” phrasing for Okomfo Anokye further aligns with the request. - Buganda and Merina also fit the three clues very well. Buganda’s royal heritage lies in Kampala (Central Region) with British protectorate formation and early 20th-century settlement; Merina’s royal and cultural core is in Madagascar’s central highlands, with French conquest/resistance crossing the century boundary. Both can be finalized with one or two additional citations for conflict chronology and founders. - Mossi, Luba, and Sokoto plausibly fit but require precise citations for “central-region” wording and conflict date ranges before final inclusion as top matches. End of report.

Identify telecommunications experts in African countries whose names match founder/cofounder names of the shortlisted kingdoms. Focus founders: Ashanti (Osei Tutu; Okomfo Anokye), Buganda (Kato Kintu/Kintu), Merina (Andriamanelo; Andrianampoinimerina), Mossi (Ouédraogo/Ouedraogo; Yennenga; Ouedraogo), Luba (Kongolo; Ilunga), Sokoto (Usman dan Fodio/Usman). For each founder name, search for telecom experts (engineering academics, telecom regulator leaders, mobile operator executives, notable telecom technologists) in any African country sharing that name (exact full name or a distinctive component like Anokye, Tutu, Kintu, Ouedraogo, Ilunga, Usman). For each potential match, provide: (1) full name; (2) country; (3) telecom role/credentials (e.g., DG of regulator, CTO, professor of telecom engineering), with dates; (4) reliable sources (official sites, reputable news, LinkedIn/company bios, academic pages). Be inclusive: list all plausible candidates you find, but clearly flag weak/ambiguous matches (e.g., very common given names like Usman without strong telecom credentials). Prioritize confirming whether there is a Ghanaian telecom expert named Anokye (matching Okomfo Anokye) and any telecom expert named Osei Tutu; also check Ugandan telecom professionals named Kintu; check Burkina Faso telecom experts named Ouedraogo; and DRC telecom figures named Ilunga. Present a structured summary with evidence strength notes and direct links.

Joe Anokye Director-General National Communications Authority Ghana
